UsageBalanceResult.description:
An org's plan usage this period, as a share of its allowance.

There is no ``allowance_pct``: the allowance is the denominator, so it would
be 100 on every response. ``has_allowance`` is carried because both
percentages are ``"0"`` for an org that was never granted one, which is
otherwise indistinguishable from a plan spent to the last cent.

The last three describe the *next* refill, so a client can render "back to N%
in six hours" without holding a copy of either figure. All three are always
present, so there is one shape to read; the two that describe a refill are
``None`` when there is none, rather than absent.

``refresh_eligible`` is narrower than "will this allowance ever be restored":
it means the org is on the rolling refill in ``cloud.services.refills``. An
Enterprise org, still granted monthly by the billing-period reset, is False
here and the meter's own label is where its boundary is shown -- newly
exposing it under a name that says "refresh" would have a client count down
to a mechanism this field says the org is not on.

``next_refresh_at`` is an absolute UTC timestamp rather than a duration, so a
response that sat in a cache degrades into a countdown a little off rather
than one that is wrong. It is a prediction only while the org keeps coming
back: the refill is granted on the read that notices it is due, so an org
that stays away is refilled when it returns, later than this says.

``next_refresh_pct`` is what the refill is worth against the window it
replaces -- "100" in the ordinary case, because a refill sets the balance
*to* its amount, and less when the window in progress is larger than the plan
it will be replaced by (an admin adjustment). ``None`` when the org holds no
allowance for it to be a share of, the same answer ``amount_pct`` gives a
movement that predates the org's first grant. A share and not the dollars,
like every other figure on this route.
UsageBalanceResult.title: UsageBalanceResult

UsageHistoryEntry.description:
One movement against the allowance, as the usage breakdown shows it.

``amount_pct`` is the movement as a share of the grant governing its own
period, unrounded. This range is arbitrary and can span any number of plan
periods, so a single denominator would misquote every row outside the latest
one; and no fixed number of decimals survives every allowance, so a consumer
summing the column would undercount by whatever fell under the cutoff.

Not the allowance at the instant of the charge. An upgrade onto a rolling
tier opens its own window, so its movements are quoted against the plan that
funded them; a within-tier raise still edits the grant in place with no
record of the prior amount, so earlier movements in a raised window are
quoted against the raised figure. The
movements are signed, so summing them gives the remaining share rather than
the used one, and the sum is not meaningful across a plan change.
UsageHistoryEntry.title: UsageHistoryEntry

get.description:
List or filter the org's directory-owned groups.

Only ``displayName eq "..."`` is supported, which is the filter Okta and
Entra use to reconcile before create. Pagination is clamped rather than
validated, as on /Users.

post.description: Provision a group as a team. 409 uniqueness if the name is already taken.

delete.description:
Delete a group, and with it the team and every project role it held.

Permanent removal (RFC 7644 3.6): Groups carry no ``active`` attribute, so
there is no suspension to distinguish this from, and nothing is tombstoned.

patch.description:
Apply a PatchOp: ``members`` add/remove is the group-sync signal.

Okta and Entra both push membership this way, so in practice this is the
primary group path and PUT is the secondary one. The whole envelope is
folded before anything is written, so a malformed operation late in the list
cannot leave the earlier ones half-applied.

put.description:
Replace a group: renames the team and resets its member set.

``members`` is honoured only when the request carried it. An explicit empty
array empties the group; an omitted one leaves membership alone. Reading an
omission as "clear" would let a displayName-only PUT -- which is what a
client renaming a group sends -- silently revoke everyone's inherited
project access, and an IdP that means to empty a group sends ``[]``.

externalId follows the /Users rule instead: PUT replaces the resource, so an
omitted one is cleared rather than coalesced back, which both stops the
service echoing an identifier the IdP no longer holds and frees its unique
reservation for the next resource assigned it.

displayName and externalId are one team row and apply in one statement, so
a rejected identifier cannot leave a rename behind. Membership is separate
and comes last, because it is the only one of the three that moves access:
it is validated before either scalar is touched, so a member list this org
cannot accept changes nothing, and a failure in the scalars has changed
nothing a user can act with. What covers the seam that remains -- scalars
applied, membership part-applied -- is that each step is idempotent and PUT
carries the whole desired state, so a client re-driving a failed request
converges, and :func:`replace_group_members` orders its own steps to fail
closed.

get.description:
Serve the individual type the collection advertises.

A client that validates the advertised type before enabling provisioning
would otherwise get a 404 for something the collection says exists.

Return the advertised schema set.

ResourceTypes points clients here; without it a validating client can
reject the provider before it ever attempts provisioning.

Advertise supported SCIM capabilities.

Unauthenticated per RFC 7644 section 4: it describes the service, not an org.

List or filter the org's members.

Only ``userName eq "..."`` is supported, which is the filter Okta and Entra
use to reconcile before create.

Pagination is clamped rather than validated: RFC 7644 3.4.2.4 defines a
startIndex below 1 as 1 and a negative count as 0, so a zero-based client
relying on that normalization would otherwise get a 400 and never sync.

post.description:
Provision a member.

An email that is already an admin-added member is adopted into directory

patch.description:
Apply a PatchOp. ``active -> false`` is the deprovisioning signal.

Okta and Entra both soft-delete this way, so in practice this is the
primary deprovisioning path and DELETE is the secondary one. ``active ->
true`` restores a removed member on the same terms as scim_replace_user,
and identifier rotations in the same request apply with it.

put.description:
Replace a user: actuates ``active`` and persists identifier rotations.

``active: true`` for an already-removed member restores it, provided a
directory record proves this org provisioned that id -- Okta and Entra
un-suspend this way. Without such a record it stays a 404, so an id minted
by another org's directory cannot grant membership here. A DELETE removes
the record, so the resource it named is gone for good.

userName and externalId are stored on that record and rotate here; the
mailbox is the account's identity and a change to it is refused.

delete.description:
Take brokered sign-in back off the app; ``deleted`` says whether it had any.

The app stops being able to complete a sign-in, and the sessions people
were holding end. Their rows stay, so re-provisioning finds the user list
intact.

**Not gated on the flag**, unlike every route beside it, and the service is
the same way: an operator who switches brokered auth off with apps still
provisioned would otherwise be unable to take the keys back out, and those
stale app-scope keys go on shadowing any identity provider they try to
connect instead. The house rule the org surfaces follow -- a teardown is
exempt from the gate its setup sits behind, because access nobody can
revoke is worse than a control nobody can use.

get.description:

login for it. An app carrying the keys with no enabled client row refuses
every sign-in, and reported as configured it would look like nothing needed
doing -- reprovisioning is what repairs it, and both halves are idempotent.

Consent order rather than sign-in order: a returning user whose standing

``search`` narrows by address, and ``total`` narrows with it, so a client

so an unbounded needle is a sequential scan a caller chooses the cost of.

get.description:

Stopped at ``APP_USERS_EXPORT_MAX``, and a file that stopped early is named
``.partial.csv``. Truncation is decided by the walk running out of budget
rather than by comparing a count against a total, which is a second read of
a number that moves.

Switching is allowed even after the app has deployed. Moving providers
tears down what the app was running on its previous provider (so nothing
lingers or keeps billing) and demotes its deployments; the app then has to
be redeployed to come back up on the newly selected provider.

``expected_project_id`` pins the app to the project the caller acted on, in
the statement that writes. A caller working from a list of a project's apps
has read which project owns them; deploy access is checked against the app
itself, so an app that moves to another project in between would otherwise
be switched and torn down on the strength of a listing that no longer holds.

post.description:
Retry the teardown of what an app left on a provider it has already left.

Strict where the provider switch is lenient: the switch records the debt, this
settles it and fails loudly, so the project-move assistant can refuse to
proceed. Runs the whole teardown, since a debt can be recorded with none of the
stop cleanup having happened (the switch commits, then the process dies).

Works on a deleted app, which is how a delete whose teardown failed stops being
a block nobody can clear. Access is checked on the app while it exists and on
its project once it does not: a deleted app has no FGA tuple left, and the
resources are the project's to release either way.

An app still live but orphaned by its project's deletion owes nothing yet, and
has nothing left that could take its resources down -- so this finishes the
delete its project implied instead, and reports it as under way rather than
settled.

Idempotent, and safe to run on an app redeployed since the switch: the
demote/deactivate statements and the audit/CDN steps are scoped to the provider
being released, and to deployments that are still live.

get.description:
An org's ledger movements for the current month, newest first.

`amount_pct` is each movement against the grant governing its own period,
unrounded. A calendar month can span two plan periods, so one denominator
would misquote every row on the far side of the anchor; and no fixed number of
decimals survives every allowance, so a consumer summing the column would
undercount by whatever fell under the cutoff.

Not the allowance at the instant of the charge. An upgrade onto a rolling
tier opens a window of its own, so its movements are quoted against the plan
that funded them; a within-tier raise still edits the grant in place
(`raise_period_reset_amount_query`) with no record of the prior amount, so
movements made earlier in a raised window read against the raised figure.

The movements are signed, so summing them gives the *remaining* share, not the
used one: a period that grants 100.00 and spends 20.00 sums to 80.00. Nor is
the sum meaningful across a plan change, since each row is a share of its own
allowance.

Carries no attribution beyond the movement itself. The ledger's thread
columns are gated on the caller's project access, which this route does not
resolve, and a task debit's notes name the models a generation used -- ours
to know rather than a customer's to read.

post.description:
Dry-run a role edit: what its holders would gain and lose, and who they are.

Writes nothing. The same validation as the real edit runs first, so a
preview of a request that would be rejected is an error rather than a diff
the caller could never apply.

A preview is point-in-time and the save re-checks everything, so a change
landing in between still wins. Reading the primary rather than a replica
only keeps the two from disagreeing over replication lag as well.

get.description: The teams holding a role on the project, plus the changes awaiting approval.

delete.description:
Take away the role *team_id* holds on the project.

Idempotent in the same way as the grant: a team that holds no role is
already in the desired state and answers ``not_granted``, while a team id
that resolves to nothing is a 404, since that is a caller error rather than
a converged reconcile. ``pending_approval`` means the revocation parked --
the team keeps its access until an approver accepts.

put.description:
Give *team_id* the named role on the project, or change the one it holds.

Idempotent, because a provisioner asserts desired state rather than diffing
first: re-granting the role a team already holds succeeds. ``status``
separates ``granted`` from ``pending_approval`` -- a project whose
PROJECT_MEMBER_GRANT gate is on parks the grant instead of applying it, and
a caller that read 200 as "the access exists" would record access nobody has
yet.

get.description:
List the caller's tokens, without their values.

The ids are dropped rather than never selected: they are the bearer
credentials, and every one of them is reveal-once, so returning them here
would let any authenticated full-access session read back every active token
it has ever created. The query carries them for the in-process caller above,
which needs them to resolve its own row handles and never sends them on.

How much of the org's plan this period has used, and how much is left.

Replaces ``/credits/balance``. Reports the share rather than the money: the
dollar amount behind an allowance is ours, and the percentage is what the
product tells the customer everywhere it is asked.

Itemized movements against the allowance over a date range.

Replaces ``/credits/history``. No ``project_id``: the ledger is org-keyed and
carries no project, so a project-scoped answer would be a fabrication rather
than a filter.

One page at a time. Hosting is metered hourly, so a default 30-day window is
thousands of movements for an org running a handful of apps and a single
response could only ever be the newest few hundred of them. When more remain,
``X-Next-Cursor`` carries the token that opens the following page — a header
rather than a wrapper object, so a client written against the bare list this
has always returned reads the same first page it always did, and one that
wants the whole window can now reach the end of it.

Args:
    start_date: ISO date or datetime. Defaults to 30 days ago. Ignored on a
        continuation, which keeps the lower bound its walk began under.
    end_date: ISO date or datetime. Defaults to tomorrow; a date-only value
        keeps its inclusive-day meaning.
    cursor: The ``X-Next-Cursor`` of the previous page. Omit for the newest.
